title: Ginzburg Publishes Ecstasies: Shamanic Substrate Theory for the Witches' Sabbath
description:
Carlo Ginzburg's Ecstasies: Deciphering the Witches' Sabbath, published in Italian in 1989 and in English translation in 1991, was his most ambitious and controversial work, extending the argument developed in The Night Battles (1966/1983) into a grand historical thesis about the origins of the witches' sabbath. Ginzburg argued that the sabbath narrative — the stereotyped description of nocturnal gatherings, animal transformation, and demonic contact — derived not from elite theological invention but from a stratum of folk belief ultimately rooted in ancient Eurasian shamanic practices. Drawing on comparative evidence from Celtic myths, Germanic folklore, Siberian shamanism, and diverse European folk traditions, Ginzburg traced morphological parallels that he argued pointed toward a common cultural substratum underlying the apparently disparate materials.

The reception of Ecstasies was considerably more divided than the reception of The Night Battles. Ginzburg's comparative morphological method — finding structural parallels across cultures widely separated in time and space and inferring common origin — was criticized by scholars including Bob Scribner, Wolfgang Behringer, and others as methodologically unsound: structural similarities need not imply common origin and could reflect independent convergence or general human cognitive tendencies. The scope of the argument, spanning millennia and continents, struck many historians as exceeding what the evidence could support. Stuart Clark in Thinking with Demons expressed skepticism about whether the folk beliefs underlying confessions needed a shamanic explanation when simpler accounts were available.

Despite critical reception among historians, Ecstasies had considerable influence in comparative religion and folklore studies, where the search for structural parallels across traditions was more methodologically accepted. The work has been particularly influential in discussions of ecstatic practices in shamanism and their possible connections to European folk religion. Emma Wilby's work on Isobel Gowdie drew on Ginzburg's framework in a more cautious and specific way, arguing for connections between Scottish folk practice and shamanic-type traditions while not endorsing Ginzburg's grandest claims.
historiographical_note: The scholarly reception of Ecstasies was sharply divided. Favorable reception came from comparative religionists and folklorists who found Ginzburg's morphological method productive; critical reception from social historians who found the comparisons too speculative. Stuart Clark's brief engagement in Thinking with Demons is characteristically precise: he accepts that folk beliefs existed but questions whether the shamanic interpretation is necessary. Wolfgang Behringer's critiques focused on the methodological problems of cross-cultural morphological comparison. Emma Wilby's more cautious version of the argument in Cunning Folk and Familiar Spirits represents a middle position.
source_method: Primary scholarship (Ginzburg, Ecstasies, 1991 [Italian 1989]); scholarly reviews and responses
